title: Revascularization of Asymptomatic Carotid Artery Stenosis
abstract: Importance: Studies show that asymptomatic carotid artery stenosis is associated with diminished cognition. Whether carotid revascularization leads to cognitive improvement is unclear. Objective: To determine whether carotid revascularization improves cognition. Design, Setting, and Participants: Prespecified cognitive secondary outcomes of the CREST-2 randomized clinical trials of patients 35 years or older with 70% or greater asymptomatic carotid stenosis. Enrollment was December 2014 through July 2024, and follow-up ended July 2025. Five cognitive tests were administered before treatment and annually up to 4 years. Cognitive performances from 146 clinical sites were centrally assessed by telephone, blinded to treatment. Interventions: Two trials compared carotid stenting plus intensive medical management (CAS + IMM) with IMM alone and carotid endarterectomy plus IMM (CEA + IMM) with IMM alone. Main Outcomes and Measures: Five cognitive tests, assessing learning, memory, executive function, attention, and processing speed, administered to all patients, were assessed for unadjusted and adjusted mean z scores using a linear mixed model. The minimal clinically important difference was 0.50 SD between treatment groups. The prespecified primary analysis was the fully adjusted composite z score at 4 years. Secondary analyses assessed the individual tests and at the test intervals. Results: Among 2366 US study patients, 2165 (91.5%) participated in cognitive assessments, 1078 in the CAS trial (529 CAS + IMM; 549 IMM alone) and 1087 in the CEA trial (543 CEA + IMM; 544 IMM alone); mean age was 70.1 years (SD, 7.7) and 37.8% were female. Following baseline, 4954 test batteries were administered for a mean of 2.24 (SD, 1.09) follow-up years. There were no treatment-related differences in the fully adjusted estimated composite z scores at 4 years for either the CAS trial (CAS + IMM, 0.22 [95% CI, 0.13 to 0.30] vs IMM alone, 0.18 [95% CI, 0.09 to 0.27]; between-group difference, 0.03 [95% CI, −0.09 to 0.15]) or the CEA trial (CEA + IMM, 0.25 [95% CI, 0.17 to 0.33] vs IMM, 0.23 [95% CI, 0.15 to 0.32]; between-group difference, 0.02 [95% CI, −0.09 to 0.14]). There were no significant differences between revascularization plus medical management vs IMM alone for any individual cognitive test. Conclusions and Relevance: In patients with severe asymptomatic carotid artery stenosis, revascularization with either CAS or CEA plus IMM, compared with IMM alone, did not significantly improve cognitive function at up to 4 years of follow-up.

ai_takeaways.conclusion_vi: In patients with severe asymptomatic carotid stenosis, neither carotid stenting nor endarterectomy plus intensive medical management significantly improved cognitive function compared with intensive medical management alone at 4 years (CAS difference, 0.03 [95% CI, −0.09 to 0.15]; CEA difference, 0.02 [95% CI, −0.09 to 0.14]).

title: Revascularization in Asymptomatic Carotid Artery Stenosis With Hemodynamic Impairment and Cognitive Outcomes
abstract: Importance: Cerebral hemodynamic impairment in patients with asymptomatic internal carotid artery (ICA) stenosis is associated with reduced cognition. It is uncertain whether revascularization might be an effective treatment for cognitive impairment in these patients. Objective: To test whether any cognitive benefit from revascularization of high-grade, asymptomatic ICA stenosis varies based on the degree of baseline cerebral hemodynamic impairment. Design, Setting, and Participants: This substudy was conducted within a multicenter phase 3 randomized clinical trial. Adults (aged 35-86 years) without dementia with eighth-grade education or higher and unilateral asymptomatic ICA stenosis greater than or equal to 70% were enrolled from January 2018 to July 2024 at 61 sites in North America (last follow-up in July 2025). Of 607 participants screened from 2485 in CREST-2, 392 were enrolled. Magnetic resonance or computed tomographic perfusion imaging tested for baseline hemodynamic impairment defined by delayed time-to-peak (TTP) arrival of intravenous contrast in the hemisphere ipsilateral minus contralateral to the stenotic artery. Intervention: Carotid revascularization (endarterectomy or stenting) plus intensive medical management (IMM) vs IMM alone. Main Outcomes and Measures: The primary outcome was the difference in composite cognitive z score over 1 year based on 5 cognitive tests. The primary analysis tested for an interaction between treatment group (revascularization vs IMM alone) and degree of baseline hemodynamic impairment among those with reduced baseline cognition (cognitive z score ≤−1.0 SD). Results: Of 392 participants enrolled (mean age, 71 years; 125 [32%] females), 61 were excluded for missing baseline imaging and 40 for missing cognitive examinations or other covariates, leaving 291 with complete data. Fifty-one had reduced cognition at baseline (25 in the revascularization group and 26 in the IMM alone group). TTP ranged from no interhemispheric TTP delay to a more-than-2-second delay. Mean (SD) cognitive z scores were −1.36 (0.51) at baseline and −1.17 (0.47) at 1 year in the revascularization group and −1.34 (0.83) at baseline and −1.01 (0.97) at 1 year in the IMM alone group. The primary analysis showed no difference in cognition by treatment group over 1 year, adjusting for treatment group × hemodynamic status interaction and other covariates (adjusted difference in cognitive z score, −0.15 SD [95% CI, −0.54 to 0.24]). The interaction was not significant (β estimate = 0.018 [95% CI, −0.025 to 0.061]; P = .40). Conclusions and Relevance: In this substudy of a randomized clinical trial, there was no differential effect of revascularization vs IMM alone on cognition over 1 year by cerebral hemodynamic status among those with baseline reduced cognition, suggesting that revascularization does not improve cognitive dysfunction by restoring flow to the brain in chronic asymptomatic carotid stenosis. Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03121209

ai_takeaways.conclusion_vi: Among adults with asymptomatic high-grade carotid stenosis and baseline cognitive impairment, carotid revascularization plus intensive medical management versus medical management alone did not improve 1-year cognitive outcomes, showing no significant treatment-by-hemodynamic-status interaction (adjusted difference in cognitive z score, -0.15 SD [95% CI, -0.54 to 0.24]; P = .40).

title: Rate and Shape of Functional Decline in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Identify Clinically Distinct Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Phenotypes
abstract: Objective: The ALS Functional Rating Scale–Revised decline rate compresses trajectory shape into a single number, potentially missing distinct phenotypes. We tested whether shape identifies phenotypes that rate does not distinguish, and whether post‐hoc analysis recovers a hidden ultrarapid subgroup. Methods: From the Piemonte and Valle d'Aosta register (2000–2022), we applied 2 models to 1,686 amyotrophic lateral sclerosis patients: a Gaussian mixture model (GMM; rate axis) and a latent‐class mixed model (LCMM) with cubic splines (shape axis). Concordance, prognostic performance, calibration, and clinical utility were assessed at 24 months. External validation used the Emilia‐Romagna register. Results: The rate model identified 4 classes (GMM‐Slow 31%, GMM‐Inter‐slow 46%, GMM‐Inter‐fast 17%, GMM‐Catastrophic 6%; slopes −0.44 to −3.52 points/month); the shape model 4 (LCMM‐SlowLinear 46%, LCMM‐PlateauFall 23%, LCMM‐LateDecline 15%, LCMM‐RapidEarly 16%). Concordance was modest (kappa = 0.273). Adding shape to rate changed discrimination negligibly (C‐index 0.761 vs 0.755), but separated subgroups within rate classes (within GMM‐Catastrophic, 30.1 vs 12.0 months). LCMM‐LateDecline combined moderate early decline with reduced respiratory reserve (median forced vital capacity 83.5%) and 22.7‐month median survival. The combined model gave the greatest net benefit for the composite outcome. Of 945 patients excluded for sparse sampling, 367 were ultrarapid progressors with shorter survival than LCMM‐RapidEarly; findings replicated in the Emilia‐Romagna register. Interpretation: Rate and shape describe partially overlapping aspects of the disease. LCMM‐LateDecline, with moderate early decline yet occult respiratory compromise, is clinically challenging, and the 3‐visit criterion hides over half of ultrarapid patients. Rate predicts the overall burden of progression, whereas shape predicts the timing of deterioration. ANN NEUROL 2026

ai_takeaways.conclusion_vi: While overall functional decline rate predicts total disease burden, trajectory shape captures the timing of deterioration. Combining rate and shape models identifies clinically distinct amyotrophic lateral sclerosis phenotypes—such as occult respiratory compromise in late-decline patients—improving prognostic utility beyond standard rate-based assessments alone.

title: Gain-of-Function Variants in PLAAT4 and Spinal Predominant Demyelinating Leukodystrophy
abstract: Importance: Leukoencephalopathies are clinically and etiologically heterogeneous disorders, and establishing a specific diagnosis remains challenging. Patients with unexplained spastic paraplegia and brain white matter hyperintensities (WMH) may be misdiagnosed as having multiple sclerosis, potentially exposing them to unnecessary immunosuppressive therapy. Objective: To define the clinical, radiological, and genetic features of spinal predominant demyelinating leukodystrophy with leg spasticity (SPDMLS). Design, Setting, and Participants: This case series involved participants from 4 tertiary referral hospitals within the China Alliance for Rare Diseases during the period July 2019 to August 2025. The study design integrated clinical evaluations and whole-exome sequencing (WES), as well as targeted plasma lipidomics correlated with SPATAX-EUROSPA disability stages. Variant pathogenicity was evaluated using an oligodendrocyte-specific knock-in mouse model. Participants were patients with unexplained spastic paraplegia and central nervous system (CNS) WMH and available family members, including presymptomatic carriers. Exposures: WES, genetic characterization, testing. Main Outcomes and Measures: Identification of disease-associated gene and characterization of clinical, radiological, and genetic features of SPDMLS. Results: Twenty-six individuals from 11 unrelated families were included; 4 patients underwent longitudinal follow-up for up to 5 years. Recurrent heterozygous PLAAT4 (phospholipase A and acyltransferase 4) variants (p.I14T and p.A96V) were associated with a novel autosomal dominant leukoencephalopathy, named SPDMLS. Age at onset was 11 to 51 years (median [IQR], 22 [15-29] years), with patients predominantly developing spastic paraplegia. Symbol Digit Modalities Test scores ranged from 11 to 70 in 6 available patients. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated slow progression with heterogeneous brain WMH and a stereotyped pattern of symmetric, long-segment “girdle-like” spinal cord WMH accompanied by atrophy. Somatosensory- and motor-evoked potentials indicated dysfunction of the dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts, respectively. In presymptomatic carriers, spinal cord signal alterations preceded brain involvement. An oligodendrocyte-specific knock-in mouse model provided in vivo functional evidence supporting a role of PLAAT4 gain-of-function in driving demyelination, informing SPDMLS pathogenesis. Patient plasma lipidomics suggested accumulation of arachidonic acid–related lipids correlating with disability stage. Conclusions and Relevance: This study found that PLAAT4 variants delineated SPDMLS, a clinically distinct leukodystrophy that should be considered in patients with unexplained spastic paraplegia and CNS WMH. Arachidonic acid–related lipids represent a candidate biomarker for disease progression.

ai_takeaways.conclusion_vi: Heterozygous gain-of-function PLAAT4 variants cause spinal predominant demyelinating leukodystrophy with leg spasticity (SPDMLS), a distinct autosomal dominant leukodystrophy mimicking multiple sclerosis. Practicing neurologists should consider SPDMLS—characterized by stereotyped long-segment spinal cord white matter hyperintensities and elevated arachidonic acid-related lipids tracking disability—in patients with unexplained spastic paraplegia and central nervous system white matter hyperintensities.

title: Changing Patterns of Transient Ischemic Attack Evaluation in US Emergency Departments
abstract: Importance: For US patients presenting to the emergency department (ED) with transient ischemic attack (TIA), guidelines recommend resource-intensive multimodal evaluation to optimize secondary stroke prevention. These resources are not available in all EDs, and national patterns of ED TIA care are not well described. Objectives: To evaluate national trends in ED TIA care, including discharge practices, imaging use, and associated costs, and to assess patient- and hospital-level factors associated with these patterns. Design, Setting, and Participants: This was a retrospective repeated cross-sectional study of ED visits using the 2013-2021 National Emergency Department Sample of the Healthcare Cost and Utilization Project, a weighted, nationally representative annual sample of ED visits in the US. TIA and stroke encounters during the study period were identified among patients aged 18 years or older by a first-listed International Classification of Diseases, Ninth Revision or Tenth Revision code for TIA or stroke diagnosis. Analyses were performed from October 2024 to April 2026. Exposures: Calendar year. Main Outcomes and Measures: ED discharge; imaging use among discharged TIA encounters; and inflation-adjusted ED cost per discharged encounter. Results: This study included 2 151 408 (95% CI, 2 107 855-2 194 960) weighted ED visits for TIA (1 194 630 [55.5%] female; mean [SEM] age, 69.8 [0.05] years). Adjusted models found the predicted probability of discharge increased from 45% (95% CI, 43%-46%) in 2013 to 66% (95% CI, 64%-68%) in 2021 ( P < .001 for trend). During this time, mean ED charges increased from 1746 (95% CI, 1662-1830) to 2755 (95% CI, 2674-2836) per encounter ( P < .001 for trend). Imaging use among discharged TIA encounters increased substantially, including computed tomography angiography (predicted probability, 4% [95% CI, 3%-4%] in 2013 vs 45% [95% CI, 42%-47%] in 2021; P < .001 for trend) and magnetic resonance imaging (predicted probability, 17% [95% CI, 16%-19%] in 2013 vs 53% [95% CI, 50%-55%] in 2021; P < .001 for trend). Rate of discharge was higher in rural encounters than in urban encounters for all years studied, and the rate of magnetic resonance imaging use was lower. Conclusions and Relevance: This cross-sectional study demonstrates a shift in TIA care over time that suggests increased use of the ED to expedite evaluation for TIA that previously occurred during a brief hospitalization. This approach has consequences in terms of cost and ED throughput and may not be as feasible in rural hospitals as it is in urban hospitals.

ai_takeaways.conclusion_vi: Between 2013 and 2021, US emergency department discharges for transient ischemic attack increased from 45% (95% CI, 43%-46%) to 66% (95% CI, 64%-68%; P < .001), alongside rising costs and increased use of CT angiography (4% to 45%; P < .001) and MRI (17% to 53%; P < .001), highlighting an outpatient-oriented shift with disparities in rural settings.

title: Internet Intervention for Functional Seizures
abstract: Importance: Functional seizures (FS) are a common and disabling presentation in neurology clinics, but evidence-based treatments are difficult to access in Australia and in many regions globally. A brief, scalable, internet-delivered intervention could narrow this treatment gap. Objective: To compare a self-guided and a therapist-guided internet-based intervention for FS, each delivered alongside standard care, with standard care alone. Design, Setting, and Participants: This was a 3-arm, parallel, randomized clinical trial conducted between February 2022 and April 2024, with follow-up through to 12 months after randomization. The location was a specialist outpatient clinic in Melbourne, Australia. Included were adults (≥18 years) with a documented diagnosis of FS confirmed by video electroencephalogram monitoring and at least 4 seizures per month, excluding comorbid active epilepsy. Interventions: Participants were randomized 1:1:1 to a self-guided internet-based intervention plus standard care, therapist-guided internet-based intervention plus standard care, or standard care alone. Re-PROGRAM is an internet-based intervention developed for FS, comprising 5 structured sessions integrating lifestyle factors, seizure management techniques, and elements of cognitive behavioral, acceptance and commitment, and dialectical behavior therapy. Main Outcomes and Measures: The primary outcome was monthly seizure frequency at 6 weeks, 6 months, and 12 months after randomization, recorded by daily prospective seizure diary, with retrospective estimates used for incomplete records. Secondary outcomes included depression, anxiety, quality of life, psychosocial functioning, and somatic symptoms. Results: Of 220 individuals screened for eligibility, 107 (mean [SD] age 36.0 [12.4] years; 89 female [83%]) were randomized. Of these participants, 96 contributed to the full analysis set (29 self-guided, 34 therapist-guided, 33 standard care). The self-guided arm produced significantly greater overall reductions in monthly seizure frequency than standard care (rate ratio [RR], 0.35; 95% CI, 0.18-0.69; Holm-Bonferroni [HB] method P = .006), with sustained between-group effects at 6 weeks (RR, 0.37; 95% CI, 0.18-0.76; HB P = .02), 6 months (RR, 0.31; 95% CI, 0.12-0.78; HB P = .04), and 12 months (RR, 0.35; 95% CI, 0.16-0.78; HB P = .03). The self-guided arm also showed greater improvements in anxiety than standard care at all 3 time points and in depression and mental quality of life at 1 or more time points. The therapist-guided arm showed greater improvement in anxiety at 6 months, but reductions in seizure frequency did not reach statistical significance. Direct comparison between the 2 active arms showed no significant difference in seizure reduction (RR, 0.67; 95% CI, 0.33-1.36). Sensitivity analyses confirmed robustness of the primary findings. No adverse events occurred in any arm. Conclusions and Relevance: Results of this randomized clinical trial show that in adults with FS, a self-guided internet-based intervention reduced seizure frequency and improved anxiety relative to standard care, offering a scalable option for patients unable to access specialist psychological care. Trial Registration: Identifier: ACTRN12622000262707

ai_takeaways.conclusion_vi: For adults with functional seizures, a self-guided internet-based intervention plus standard care significantly reduced monthly seizure frequency compared with standard care alone (RR, 0.35; 95% CI, 0.18-0.69; Holm-Bonferroni P = .006) with sustained effects through 12 months, offering a scalable treatment option when specialist psychological care is inaccessible.

title: Cytoprotection for Acute Ischemic Stroke: Critical Appraisal of Recent Clinical Trials
abstract: Several phase III clinical trials testing cytoprotective approaches have recently been completed, and many of these studies report a clinical benefit. Reviewing the outcomes of these trials in light of their specific designs reveals intriguing results. Trials designed with shorter treatment time windows (≤24 hours) and featuring high rates of recanalization therapies predominantly show neutral outcomes, that is, no therapeutic benefit. Studies using later time points (>24 hours to 14 days) and often enrolling patients in whom recanalization is not or only infrequently established show clear treatment effects. These results challenge our current understanding of cytoprotective approaches, which are believed to primarily target the penumbra as the key to therapeutic success. The reasons for this are unclear. They may include other, potentially unknown mechanisms of action that improve clinical outcome even when applied within longer time windows rather than exerting acute cytoprotection. Here, we discuss such potential mechanisms, to what extent they could explain the results of recent cytoprotection trials, and review consequences for future translational and clinical research.

ai_takeaways.conclusion_vi: Recent stroke trials testing cytoprotection in patients with high recanalization rates and shorter time windows (≤24 hours) showed neutral outcomes, whereas studies using later time windows (>24 hours to 14 days) with infrequent recanalization demonstrated clear treatment effects, suggesting mechanisms beyond acute penumbral salvage.

title: Differences in Epilepsy Etiology, Type, Syndrome, and Severity Between Māori and Non-Māori-Non-Pasifika Children With Epilepsy in New Zealand
abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: The World Health Organization's Intersectoral Global Action Plan on Epilepsy and other Neurologic Disorders 2022-2031 aims to minimize epilepsy burden, with an emphasis on Indigenous peoples. Māori, the Indigenous peoples of New Zealand, have a similar prevalence of treated epilepsy to non-Māori yet suffer an increased epilepsy burden. This study aims to describe epilepsy etiology, syndrome, and severity in Māori children compared with non-Māori-non-Pasifika children. METHODS: Retrospective population-based study using the New Zealand Pharmaceutical Collection. Medical records were reviewed to compare epilepsy etiology, type, syndrome, and severity between Māori and age-matched and sex-matched non-Māori-non-Pasifika children (younger than 18 years) with treated epilepsy. Period prevalence of etiology was compared: logistic regression (odds ratio, OR) for comparisons of within-cohort proportions and Poisson regression (rate ratio, RR) for comparison of population prevalence. RESULTS: Cohort of 337 Māori and 421 non-Māori-non-Pasifika children (female: 45.4% Māori and 46.6% non-Māori-non-Pasifika). The median age of first seizure was 3.0 years for Māori (interquartile range [IQR]: 0.9-8.0) and 4.0 years for non-Māori-non-Pasifika (IQR: 1.3-8.0). Māori children were more likely to live in high deprivation areas (quintile 5: 48.4% Māori vs 17.3% non-Māori-non-Pasifika). Māori children were more likely to have a preventable cause of their epilepsy than non-Māori-non-Pasifika children (RR: 2.32; 95% CI 1.41-3.80) and more likely to have a structural (RR: 1.43, 95% CI 1.04-1.97) or infectious (RR: 4.72, 95% CI 1.43-15.8) etiology. After adjustment for socioeconomic status and rurality, there was no longer evidence for a difference by ethnicity. Focal epilepsy was the most common epilepsy type (65.6% Māori and 59.4% non-Māori-non-Pasifika), followed by genetic epilepsies (20.2% Māori and 21.9% non-Māori-non-Pasifika). An epilepsy syndrome was identified in 26% of Māori and 36% of non-Māori-non-Pasifika children. Māori children were less likely to have a self-limited epilepsy syndrome (OR: 0.51, 95% CI 0.30-0.83) or developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (OR: 0.59, 95% CI 0.40-0.88) but more likely to have intellectual disability and epilepsy (OR: 1.65, 95% CI 1.18-2.32). DISCUSSION: Health inequities exist for Māori children who are twice as likely to have preventable epilepsy than non-Māori-non-Pasifika children. This inequity is largely driven by socioeconomic status and rurality.

ai_takeaways.conclusion_vi: Māori children with epilepsy experience significantly higher rates of preventable (RR: 2.32; 95% CI 1.41-3.80), structural, and infectious etiologies compared with non-Māori-non-Pasifika children, disparities that are largely mediated by socioeconomic status and rurality rather than ethnicity alone.

title: Anticoagulation in Atrial Fibrillation With Previous Intracranial Bleeding
abstract: Background and objectives: Patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) and previous intracranial bleeding are at high risk of ischemic and bleeding events, and the benefits and risks of oral anticoagulation (OAC) remain uncertain. We investigated competing risks of recurrent intracranial bleeding, ischemic stroke (IS), and death from other causes according to anticoagulation strategy. Methods: This nationwide Finnish cohort study using linked administrative registries included patients with first-ever AF diagnosed in 2010-2018 and intracranial bleeding at least 120 days earlier. Follow-up began 90 days after AF diagnosis. Patients were categorized as receiving direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs), warfarin, or no OAC based on drug purchases. Warfarin users were further stratified by time in therapeutic range (TTR). Inverse probability of treatment weighting balanced baseline characteristics. Competing risks were analyzed using adjusted cumulative incidence functions and cause-specific Cox regression. Results: Among 1,502 patients (median age 78 years [IQR 71-85], 44% female, 41% with only traumatic intracranial bleeding), 15% received DOACs, 29% warfarin, and 56% no OAC. At 1 year, adjusted absolute risks of IS were 0.7%, 2.1%, and 4.1%; intracranial bleeding, 1.2%, 2.7%, and 1.9%; and death from other causes, 4.7%, 8.6%, and 14.7%, respectively. Compared with no OAC, DOAC use was associated with lower risks of IS (HR 0.17, 95% CI 0.04-0.71) and death (HR 0.20, 95% CI 0.09-0.46) without increased intracranial bleeding risk (HR 0.70, 95% CI 0.19-2.50). Warfarin use was associated with lower risks of IS (HR 0.49, 95% CI 0.26-0.93) and death (HR 0.60, 95% CI 0.44-0.80), but increased intracranial bleeding risk (HR 1.85, 95% CI 1.01-3.41). Among warfarin users, TTR ≥70% was associated with lower risks of IS (HR 0.24, 95% CI 0.08-0.79) and death (HR 0.19, 95% CI 0.10-0.36); associations were attenuated with poorer or missing TTR. Discussion: In patients with AF and previous intracranial bleeding, OAC was associated with lower risks of IS and death. DOAC use was not associated with increased intracranial bleeding risk, whereas warfarin use was. Limited information on previous intracranial bleeding and potential residual confounding warrant cautious interpretation. These findings support individualized anticoagulation decisions in this high-risk population.

ai_takeaways.conclusion_vi: In atrial fibrillation patients with prior intracranial bleeding, DOACs reduced ischemic stroke (HR 0.17, 95% CI 0.04-0.71) and death (HR 0.20, 95% CI 0.09-0.46) without increasing intracranial bleeding (HR 0.70, 95% CI 0.19-2.50) compared to no OAC, whereas warfarin increased bleeding risk (HR 1.85, 95% CI 1.01-3.41).

title: Blood-Based Biomarkers as Predictors of All-Cause Dementia
abstract: Background and objectives: Blood-based biomarkers are strongly correlated with amyloid positivity in research settings, but their long-term performance in heterogeneous populations remains unclear. Our aim was to determine their long-term prediction accuracy for incident all-cause dementia on their own and when used alongside known risk factors in community-dwelling older adults. Methods: This was a retrospective study based on the UK Whitehall II longitudinal, population-based cohort study established in 1985 among civil servants that includes a clinical examination every 4-5 years. Blood samples stored at the 2013-2013 wave were assayed in 2024 for measures of amyloid-beta (Aβ) 42 and 40, glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), neurofilament light (NfL), and phosphorylated tau protein 217 (p-tau217). Incident all-cause dementia, from 2012 to 2013 to 2025, was ascertained from linked medical records, and Cox regression was used to examine associations of biomarkers with dementia, followed by estimation of prediction statistics. Results: Of the 5,225 (27.2% female) participants (mean age in 2012-2013, 69.4 ± 5.7 years), 516 (30.0% female) had a dementia diagnosis over a 12.2-year median follow-up. Participants with values in the worst quartile of amyloid-beta 42 (Aβ42)/40 ratio (hazard ratio [HR] 1.88; 95% CI 1.57-2.24), p-tau217 (HR 3.74; 95% CI 3.12-4.50), NfL (HR 1.88; 95% CI 1.56-2.28), and GFAP (HR 2.25; 95% CI 1.87-2.72) had higher risk of dementia. The C-index for predicting dementia was highest for p-tau217 (0.693; 95% CI 0.672-0.714), lowest for Aβ42/40 ratio (0.587; 95% CI 0.566-0.608), and was 0.760 (0.738, 0.781) for all biomarkers together. Sensitivity (between 41.7% and 59.5%) and positive predictive value (between 16.4% and 23.5%) of all biomarkers were modest, but specificity (between 76.8% and 78.8%) and negative predictive value (92.3%-94.7%) were good. A second approach to prediction modeling showed a model containing sociodemographic, behavioral, and health-related risk factors to have a C-index of 0.765 (95% CI 0.746-0.785); adding all biomarkers to this model led to a C-index of 0.813 (95% CI 0.795-0.830). Discussion: The long-term predictive ability of blood-based biomarkers for incident dementia in community-dwelling older adults was modest due to poor sensitivity and similar to that of a model containing known risk factors.

ai_takeaways.conclusion_vi: In community-dwelling older adults, blood-based biomarkers demonstrate modest long-term prediction for incident all-cause dementia (C-index 0.760; 95% CI 0.738–0.781 for all markers combined). Adding all biomarkers to a model of established sociodemographic, behavioral, and health-related risk factors only marginally improves the C-index from 0.765 (95% CI 0.746–0.785) to 0.813 (95% CI 0.795–0.830).

title: Association Between Epilepsy and Young-Onset Dementia
abstract: Background and objectives: Epilepsy is linked to late-onset dementia, but evidence for young-onset dementia (YOD; Methods: We conducted 3 nationwide analyses. A French nested case-control analysis included patients with incident YOD aged 40-64 years, diagnosed between January 1, 2016, and December 31, 2018. Index date was the first YOD-related health care event; controls were risk-set matched on age, sex, and region. A Swedish nested case-control replication included patients with YOD diagnosed between January 1, 1987, and December 31, 2016, with matched controls. In both studies, epilepsy-related diagnoses and antiseizure medication (ASM) dispensations were assessed up to 10 years before index date. Odds ratios (ORs) were estimated with conditional logistic regression. A French retrospective cohort included adults aged 30-55 years with incident epilepsy in 2008, matched to individuals with prevalent epilepsy before 2008 or no epilepsy. The cohort index was the first ASM reimbursement in the incident epilepsy group or the matched date for comparators. Follow-up ended at YOD, death, or 10 years. We estimated 10-year cumulative incidence and adjusted (comorbidities, deprivation) hazard ratios (HRs), treating death as a competing event. Sensitivity analyses included lagged entry up to 5 years. Results: Case-control studies included 11,360 cases and 113,600 controls in France and 16,433 cases and 164,330 controls in Sweden. In France, 12.5% of YOD cases vs 1.2% of controls had previous epilepsy-related codes (adjusted OR 3.76, 95% CI 3.42-4.14), and 27.3% vs 10.3% had ASM dispensations (adjusted OR 1.44, 95% CI 1.36-1.52). The French cohort included 12,901 individuals with incident epilepsy, 64,083 with prevalent epilepsy, and 129,010 without epilepsy (mean age 44.0 years; 55.5% female participants). Ten-year cumulative YOD incidence was 2.20% (95% CI 1.94-2.48) with incident epilepsy (adjusted HR compared with individuals without epilepsy 6.02, 95% CI 4.98-7.26), 1.74% (1.64-1.85) with prevalent epilepsy (adjusted HR 5.38, 95% CI 4.64-6.25), and 0.21% (0.19-0.24) without epilepsy. Associations attenuated with longer lags but persisted beyond 5 years. Discussion: Across 2 countries and complementary designs, epilepsy was strongly associated with YOD. Epilepsy conferred higher YOD risk in midlife, especially with multimorbidity, supporting epilepsy inclusion in YOD risk stratification and prevention.

ai_takeaways.conclusion_vi: Epilepsy is strongly associated with young-onset dementia (YOD) in midlife. Incident epilepsy confers a significantly elevated 10-year risk of YOD compared to individuals without epilepsy (adjusted HR 6.02, 95% CI 4.98–7.26; 10-year cumulative incidence 2.20%), supporting the inclusion of epilepsy in YOD risk stratification and prevention strategies.
ai_takeaways.clinical_significance: Clinical significance for Epilepsy practice.

title: Association Between Plasma N-Terminal Tau, Cognitive Decline, and Neurodegeneration in the ADNI Cohort
abstract: Background and objectives: Blood-based biomarkers offer a cost-effective, minimally invasive alternative to neuroimaging and CSF biomarkers. Newly developed fluid biomarkers, including the N-terminal tau fragment (NT1), show promise for identifying individuals at risk for Alzheimer disease (AD) and for monitoring disease progression. Here, we determine whether NT1 levels are associated with key clinical and biomarker measures in a large, well-characterized cohort. Methods: Participants from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) cohort with available plasma NT1, β-amyloid (Aβ)-PET, MRI, and clinical measures (Clinical Dementia Rating) were included in this observational study. NT1 was measured using the Quanterix Simoa HD-X platform. PET, MRI, clinical, and other plasma measures were obtained using established ADNI procedures. A subset also had NULISA-based plasma measures of amyloid and tau and tau-PET assessed. Linear regression and linear mixed-effects models were used to assess cross-sectional and longitudinal associations between NT1 and clinical or biomarker measures, adjusting for relevant covariates. Multivariable-adjusted Cox regression was performed to evaluate the association between baseline NT1 levels and risk of clinically diagnosed mild cognitive impairment (MCI) or AD. Mediation analysis was conducted to examine whether hippocampal atrophy mediates the relationship between NT1 and memory decline. Spearman correlations were used to examine continuous relationships between plasma NT1 and continuous fluid and neuroimaging markers. Results: A total of 755 participants (mean age: 72.9 [7.0], female: 375 [50%]) were included in the study. Plasma NT1 levels were elevated in MCI/AD individuals (B MCI/AD [SE] = 0.09 [0.022], p = 1.98 × 10 -4 ) and were cross-sectionally associated with worse memory performance (B [SE] = -0.25 [0.09], p = 0.005). Aβ moderated the association between elevated NT1 and greater cognitive decline across multiple domains (memory: B [SE] = -0.17 [0.074], p = 0.022; executive function: B [SE] = -0.24 [0.082], p = 0.004; language: B [SE] = -0.21 [0.075], p = 0.006). NT1 levels were negatively associated with hippocampal volume (B [SE] = -264.49 [125.99], p = 0.036) and predicted longitudinal atrophy (B [SE] = -42.00 [16.90], p = 0.013). Accelerated hippocampal atrophy largely mediated the association between higher baseline NT1 level and greater memory decline (B [95% CI] indirect effect = -0.082 [-0.135 to -0.03], p = 0.003, B [95% CI] proportion mediated = 70.1% [32.6%-155.3%], p = 0.004). Higher NT1 levels were associated with higher levels of plasma biomarkers, including NULISA-based brain-derived (BD) plasma pTau (BD-pTau181, BD-pTau217, BD-pTau231: p 's -6 ) and Simoa-Based pTau181 ( p -15 ) and neurofilament light chain ( p -7 ). Discussion: Plasma NT1 may be useful in assessing amyloid-dependent cognitive decline and neurodegeneration.

ai_takeaways.conclusion_vi: Plasma N-terminal tau (NT1) is elevated in MCI/AD (p = 1.98 × 10⁻⁴) and predicts amyloid-dependent cognitive decline and hippocampal atrophy, which largely mediates memory loss (70.1% mediated, p = 0.004).
ai_takeaways.clinical_significance: Clinical significance for Cognitive & Dementia practice.

title: Association Between Systemic Fluoroquinolones and Risk of Peripheral Neuropathy
abstract: Background and objectives: Fluoroquinolone use has been associated with peripheral neuropathy in case reports, but there have been few noninterventional studies validating this association, and causality is unclear. The aim of this study was to estimate the association between systemic fluoroquinolone prescription and incident peripheral neuropathy relative to a comparator class of antibiotics, cephalosporins, using multiple databases to increase precision and assess the robustness of the results. Methods: Cohort studies were conducted using data from 2 databases of UK electronic primary care records, Clinical Practice Research Datalink Aurum and GOLD, from April 1, 1997, to December 31, 2019. Among adults (age ≥18 years) without diabetes mellitus or previously recorded peripheral neuropathy prescribed systemic fluoroquinolones or cephalosporins, hazard ratios were estimated between fluoroquinolone prescription and incident peripheral neuropathy within 60 days of prescription using stabilized inverse probability of treatment weighted Cox regression. Hazard ratios were similarly estimated for a positive control outcome of incident tendon rupture within 60 days of prescription. Risk differences for peripheral neuropathy were estimated using a weighted Aalen-Johansen estimator. Estimates were pooled across databases using fixed-effects meta-analysis. Results: In total, 2,933,982 individuals prescribed fluoroquinolones or cephalosporins in Aurum (63.7% [n = 1,868,793] female; median age 49.5 years [interquartile range (IQR) 34.1-67.5]) and 995,457 in GOLD (63.5% [n = 632,033] female, median age 51.5 years [IQR 35.6-68.0]) were included. Of these individuals, at first treatment episode, 1,002,004 (34.2%) in Aurum and 381,734 (38.3%) in GOLD were prescribed fluoroquinolones. The estimated association between fluoroquinolones and peripheral neuropathy was close to the null at first treatment episode (pooled adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] 0.96, 95% CI 0.77-1.20) and over all treatment episodes (pooled aHR 1.05, 95% CI 0.92-1.20). Hazard ratios were elevated for a positive control outcome of tendon rupture at first treatment episode (pooled aHR 1.98, 95% CI 1.55-2.53) and over all treatment episodes (1.76, 95% CI 1.52-2.04). Discussion: Findings were not indicative of a substantive difference in risk of peripheral neuropathy between those prescribed fluoroquinolones and cephalosporins. Potential residual confounding is a study limitation. Study results provide some reassurance to clinicians regarding risk of peripheral neuropathy with fluoroquinolones relative to a comparator antibiotic.

ai_takeaways.conclusion_vi: Systemic fluoroquinolone use was not associated with an increased risk of incident peripheral neuropathy compared to cephalosporins (pooled aHR 1.05, 95% CI 0.92–1.20), despite showing the expected positive control association for tendon rupture (pooled aHR 1.76, 95% CI 1.52–2.04).

title: Differential Trajectories of Brain Atrophy in Multiple Sclerosis, MOGAD, and AQP4 + NMOSD
abstract: Background and objectives: Multiple sclerosis (MS), myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated disease (MOGAD), and aquaporin-4 antibody-positive neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (AQP4 + NMOSD) are inflammatory demyelinating disorders with distinct mechanisms of tissue injury. MS is characterized by diffuse neurodegeneration, whereas damage in antibody-mediated diseases is considered attack related. In MOGAD, the relationship between disease activity and brain atrophy remains unclear. We aimed to compare longitudinal trajectories of global and regional brain atrophy across MS, MOGAD, and AQP4 + NMOSD and investigate whether atrophy in MOGAD is associated with disease course and lesion dynamics. Methods: In this retrospective multicenter Magnetic Resonance Imaging in Multiple Sclerosis (MAGNIMS) study, patients fulfilling the following criteria were enrolled: (1) age 18 years or older, (2) MS/MOGAD/AQP4 + NMOSD diagnosis, (3) ≥2 same-scanner brain MRIs ≥6 months apart and ≥3 months postattack, (4) concurrent Expanded Disability Status Scale, and (5) disease course information. White matter lesions were segmented using the Lesion Segmentation Toolbox. Longitudinal brain volumes were quantified on lesion-filled T1-weighted images using Sequence Adaptive Multimodal SEGmentation (SAMSEG) with a within-subject template approach. In MOGAD, lesion dynamics were classified as stable/new lesions/lesion resolution. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age, sex, baseline volume, and center estimated atrophy rates. Results: Overall, 489 participants from 15 centers were included (98 MS [mean age 39.79 years, 68.37% female], 72 MOGAD [42.14 years, 66.67%], 41 AQP4 + NMOSD [51.25 years, 87.80%], and 278 healthy controls [42.94 years, 61.87%]). The mean follow-up was MS: 2.44 ± 1.55 years, MOGAD: 2.57 ± 1.85, and AQP4 + NMOSD: 3.22 ± 2.42. Compared with controls, MS showed accelerated global brain atrophy (β = -2.027 cm 3 per year, 95% CI -3.430 to -0.623). MOGAD demonstrated white matter volume loss (β = -0.989, 95% CI -1.889 to -0.090) and ventricular enlargement (lateral: β = 0.219, 95% CI 0.089-0.350; third ventricle: β = 0.009, 95% CI 0.003-0.015). AQP4 + NMOSD showed pallidal volume reduction (β = -0.008, 95% CI -0.014 to -0.001). Within MOGAD, relapsing patients (62.5%) exhibited greater third ventricular expansion than MS (β = 0.009, 95% CI 0.001-0.017). MOGAD with new lesions (22.22%) had greater ventricular enlargement than controls (lateral: β = 0.359, 95% CI 0.147-0.572; third ventricle: β = 0.016, 95% CI 0.006-0.025), MS, and AQP4 + NMOSD. Discussion: Each inflammatory demyelinating disease exhibits a characteristic pattern of brain atrophy. In MOGAD, neuroaxonal loss seems associated with inflammatory activity and lesion accrual, supporting an event-driven pattern of tissue injury rather than diffuse neurodegeneration. Limitations include small NMOSD sample, heterogeneous follow-up, and potential scanner-related variability.

ai_takeaways.conclusion_vi: Multiple sclerosis, MOGAD, and AQP4+ NMOSD exhibit distinct brain atrophy trajectories. Unlike diffuse neurodegeneration in MS, MOGAD demonstrates white matter volume loss (β = -0.989, 95% CI -1.889 to -0.090) and ventricular enlargement linked to inflammatory activity and new lesion accrual, supporting an event-driven pattern of tissue injury.
ai_takeaways.clinical_significance: Clinical significance for Neuroimmunology & Neuromuscular practice.

title: Antidopaminergic Medications and Clinical Outcomes in Huntington Disease
abstract: Background and objectives: Antidopaminergic medications (ADMs), including vesicular monoamine transporter-2 (VMAT2) inhibitors and antipsychotics, are widely used to manage motor and psychiatric symptoms in Huntington disease (HD). Observational evidence suggests that ADM use may be associated with accelerated worsening of clinical outcome measures used in HD trials, but this relationship has not been examined in a controlled trial setting. We assessed the association between ADM exposure and longitudinal clinical outcomes in the Pridopidine's Outcome On Function in Huntington Disease (PROOF-HD) placebo arm. Methods: This post hoc analysis included placebo-arm participants from PROOF-HD (NCT04556656), a randomized controlled trial in adults with Total Functional Capacity (TFC) 7-13 and cytosine-adenine-guanine (CAG) ≥36. Participants were categorized as on-ADMs or off-ADMs based on concurrent medication use across the study period. Outcomes included TFC, composite Unified Huntington's Disease Rating Scale (cUHDRS), Symbol Digit Modalities Test (SDMT), Stroop Word Reading (SWR), and Total Motor Score (TMS). Primary analyses used mixed-effects models for repeated measures, corroborated by propensity score weighting (PSW) and time-varying sensitivity analyses. Results: Of 247 placebo-arm participants (mean age 52.6 years [SD 11.4]; 51% female), 135 (54.7%) were on-ADMs and 112 (45.3%) were off-ADMs. On-ADM participants demonstrated faster clinical decline across multiple outcome measures. Between-group differences in cUHDRS and TFC favored off-ADMs from weeks 39-78; at week 52, the difference in mean change was 0.66 (95% CI 0.31-1.01; p = 0.0002) for cUHDRS and 0.85 (95% CI 0.47-1.22; p Discussion: In this study of the PROOF-HD placebo arm, ADM use was associated with greater worsening across global, functional, cognitive, and motor outcome measures as compared with off-ADM participants. Residual confounding by disease severity cannot be fully excluded, although sensitivity analyses were directionally consistent. Taken together, ADM exposure, class, and dose should be systematically considered when designing and interpreting HD clinical trials. Trial registration information: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04556656. Classification of evidence: This study provides Class II evidence that in patients with HD, the use of ADMs is associated with greater worsening across global, functional, cognitive, and motor outcome measures as compared with patients not on ADMs.

ai_takeaways.conclusion_vi: In this post hoc analysis of the PROOF-HD placebo arm, antidopaminergic medication use was associated with significantly faster functional and global decline over 78 weeks (e.g., at week 52, cUHDRS mean change difference 0.66 [95% CI 0.31–1.01, *p* = 0.0002]; TFC difference 0.85 [95% CI 0.47–1.22]). Clinicians must carefully weigh ADM exposure when interpreting Huntington disease clinical trials and managing patients.
ai_takeaways.clinical_significance: Clinical significance for General Neurology practice.

title: Early Rhythm Control vs Usual Care After Acute Ischemic Stroke in Patients With Atrial Fibrillation
abstract: Background and objectives: Early rhythm control reduces cardiovascular events in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF); however, its effectiveness in the setting of acute ischemic stroke remains uncertain. We aimed to examine whether early rhythm control after acute ischemic stroke is associated with a lower risk of recurrent stroke or systemic embolism (SE) in patients with AF. Methods: This nationwide cohort study used the DeSC-IQVIA integrated database, an administrative claims database covering approximately 16 million individuals in Japan. Adults hospitalized for acute ischemic stroke with AF present at admission between 2014 and 2025 were included. The exposure was initiation of rhythm control (antiarrhythmic drugs, catheter ablation, or electrical cardioversion) within 8 weeks of admission (early rhythm control) vs no initiation (usual care), assessed at a landmark. The primary outcome was hospitalization for recurrent ischemic stroke or SE. Secondary outcomes included major bleeding, heart failure (HF) hospitalization, and all-cause mortality. Baseline differences were adjusted using propensity score overlap weighting. Cause-specific hazard ratios (HRs), cumulative incidence with death as a competing risk, and risk differences at 5 years were estimated. Results: Among 14,355 patients who survived event-free through the 8-week landmark (median age, 83 years [IQR, 78-88]; 6,935 [48.3%] women), 268 (1.9%) received early rhythm control. During 23,583 person-years, early rhythm control was associated with a lower risk of stroke/SE (HR, 0.56; 95% CI 0.32-0.97; weighted 5-year cumulative incidence, 8.0% vs 13.8%; risk difference, -5.9 percentage points [95% CI -11.0 to 0.8]). Among secondary outcomes, no association was observed with major bleeding (HR, 1.44; 95% CI 0.74-2.82) or HF hospitalization (HR, 0.73; 95% CI 0.39-1.38); early rhythm control was associated with lower all-cause mortality (HR, 0.72; 95% CI 0.53-0.97). Results were consistent across landmark periods of 4-24 weeks. Discussion: In this nationwide cohort study, early rhythm control after acute ischemic stroke in patients with AF was associated with a reduced risk of recurrent stroke or SE. These findings suggest that early rhythm control may serve as an additional secondary prevention strategy for ischemic stroke, with flexible timing of initiation. These observational findings are hypothesis-generating and warrant confirmation in randomized controlled trials.

ai_takeaways.conclusion_vi: Among acute ischemic stroke patients with atrial fibrillation, early rhythm control within 8 weeks was associated with a significantly lower risk of recurrent stroke or systemic embolism (HR, 0.56; 95% CI, 0.32-0.97) and lower all-cause mortality (HR, 0.72; 95% CI, 0.53-0.97).

title: Child Neurology: Neonatal Management of Tyrosine Hydroxylase Deficiency
abstract: Tyrosine hydroxylase deficiency is a rare, treatable, autosomal recessive disorder of monoamine neurotransmitter biosynthesis that typically presents in infancy or early childhood. Despite potential benefits of presymptomatic treatment with levodopa/carbidopa, prenatal or neonatal diagnosis remains extremely rare. We report 2 preterm neonates from unrelated families, both with known family history of tyrosine hydroxylase deficiency. After early diagnosis, levodopa/carbidopa therapy was initiated during the neonatal period. This proactive approach proved feasible and well tolerated, leading to early normalization of subtle motor abnormalities. These cases highlight the importance of early genetic diagnosis of this rare condition and the feasibility of levodopa/carbidopa treatment in neonates.

ai_takeaways.conclusion_vi: Proactive initiation of levodopa/carbidopa therapy in neonates with genetically diagnosed tyrosine hydroxylase deficiency is feasible, well-tolerated, and successfully normalizes subtle early motor abnormalities.
ai_takeaways.clinical_significance: Clinical significance for General Neurology practice.

title: Midlife and Late-Life Alzheimer Disease Blood Biomarkers and 11-Year Cognitive Decline
abstract: Background and objectives: Plasma biomarkers of Alzheimer disease (AD) neuropathology (amyloid-β42 to amyloid β40 [Aβ42/40] ratio, phosphorylated tau at threonine [p-tau181]), neurodegeneration (neurofilament light [NfL]), and neuroinflammation (glial fibrillary acidic protein [GFAP]) in late-life are associated with cognitive decline. Whether these biomarkers in midlife are predictive of subsequent cognitive decline, and whether they are associated with different cognitive domains, is uncertain. In this study, we investigated associations of midlife and late-life plasma Aβ42/40, p-tau181, NfL, and GFAP with late-life change in domain-specific (memory, language, and executive function) and global cognitive function. Methods: We performed a prospective cohort analysis of the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities Neurocognitive Study (ARIC-NCS). Outcome follow-up was from ARIC visit 5 (2011-2013) to visit 9 (2021-2022). We included all individuals from ARIC field centers (Jackson, Mississippi; Forsyth County, North Carolina; Washington County, Maryland; and Minneapolis suburbs, Minnesota) with biomarkers measured from stored specimens in midlife (visit 3, 1993-1995, mean age 59.0 years) and late-life (visit 5, 2011-2013, mean age 76.8 years). Aβ42/40, p-tau181, NfL, and GFAP were measured with the Quanterix Simoa platform and standardized to visit 3 to facilitate cross-biomarker comparisons of their rate of change from midlife to late-life. We estimated change in memory, language, executive function, and global cognition factor scores from visit 5 to visit 9 with linear mixed-effect models. Results: In 1,515 included participants, 60.7% (n = 920) were female and 25.5% (n = 387) were Black. Each SD increase in p-tau181 in midlife was significantly associated with faster late-life memory decline (β = -0.030 [95% CI -0.059 to -0.001] SD. Midlife Aβ42/40, NfL, and GFAP were not associated with subsequent decline in any cognitive domain. In late-life, p-tau181, NfL, and GFAP were significantly associated with faster decline in different cognitive domains, with the strongest associations seen with memory (β = -0.091 [95% CI -0.123 to -0.058] SD; β = -0.064 [95% CI -0.106 to -0.023] SD; and β = -0.048 [95% CI -0.082 to -0.013] SD, respectively). Discussion: Midlife p-tau181 was associated with faster 11-year memory decline beginning 20 years later in the ARIC cohort, which underscores a potentially long prodromal phase of cognitive decline that could precede dementia onset. In late-life, biomarkers for AD, neurodegeneration, and neuroinflammation were associated with faster decline across different cognitive domains, but associations remained strongest for p-tau181 and memory.

ai_takeaways.conclusion_vi: Midlife plasma p-tau181 predicts faster late-life memory decline (β = -0.030, 95% CI -0.059 to -0.001), highlighting a long prodromal phase of Alzheimer's pathology. In late-life, p-tau181, NfL, and GFAP are all associated with accelerated cognitive decline, with p-tau181 showing the strongest association with memory (β = -0.091, 95% CI -0.123 to -0.058).
ai_takeaways.clinical_significance: Clinical significance for Cognitive & Dementia practice.

title: Ambulatory Episodic Hypertension in Parkinson's Disease With Orthostatic Hypotension
abstract: Objective: The objective of this study was to determine whether ambulatory hypertensive episodes are associated with clinical outcomes in patients with Parkinson's disease (PD) with neurogenic versus non‐neurogenic orthostatic hypotension. Methods: Consecutive patients with PD with suspected orthostatic hypotension (OH) underwent 24‐hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring in the home setting. The primary exposure was the number of hypertensive episodes across 24 hours. Neurogenic OH was defined by a heart rate response to orthostatic systolic blood pressure reduction of <0.5 beats/min/mmHg during standardized 3‐minute orthostatic testing. The primary outcome was quality of life measured by the Parkinson's Disease Questionnaire‐39 Summary Index (PDQ‐39 SI). Secondary outcomes included orthostatic symptom burden and motor severity. Multivariable linear regression models with interaction terms were adjusted for age, sex, disease duration, and levodopa equivalent daily dose, with robustness assessed through multiple sensitivity analyses. Results: Fifty‐nine patients with PD were included, 30 with neurogenic OH and 29 with non‐neurogenic orthostatic hypotension. Among patients with neurogenic OH, a greater number of hypertensive episodes was associated with better quality of life, lower orthostatic symptom burden, and lower motor impairment scores. In patients with non‐neurogenic OH, these associations were absent or occurred in the opposite direction. Associations were stronger during daytime than night‐time periods and remained consistent in sensitivity analyses. Interpretation: In patients with PD and neurogenic OH, ambulatory hypertensive episodes were associated with better clinical outcomes, an association not observed in patients with non‐neurogenic OH. ANN NEUROL 2026

ai_takeaways.conclusion_vi: In Parkinson’s disease with neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, ambulatory hypertensive episodes are paradoxically associated with better quality of life, lower orthostatic symptom burden, and reduced motor impairment. Conversely, these associations are absent or reversed in patients with non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension.

title: Expanding the Evidence and Indications for Thrombectomy in Ischemic Stroke

journal.name: The New England Journal of Medicine

abstract: Mechanical thrombectomy (MT) has become the standard treatment for acute ischemic stroke (AIS) caused by large vessel occlusion, and its indications have expanded substantially over the past decade. Recent randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have extended eligibility to patients presenting in extended time windows, those with large ischemic cores, and other populations previously considered unsuitable for intervention. However, the expansion of MT indications has also raised important ethical challenges. Patients with AIS often lack decision-making capacity, requiring physicians to balance respect for patient autonomy with the principles of beneficence, nonmaleficence, and justice under severe time constraints. Moreover, RCTs have enrolled highly selected populations, and evidence remains limited for many patients encountered in clinical practice. This review discusses ethical issues related to MT across clinical contexts involving treatment beyond conventional time windows, large ischemic cores, medium or distal vessel occlusions, futile recanalization, active malignancy, and prestroke disability. Representative cases illustrate situations in which ethical considerations extend beyond guideline recommendations. Whenever possible, treatment decisions should incorporate each patient's premorbid functional status, values, anticipated quality of life, procedural risks, and expected neurological recovery. Continued evidence generation in understudied populations will be essential to support the ethically sound, patient-centered application of MT.

ai_takeaways.conclusion_vi: As mechanical thrombectomy indications expand to include extended time windows, large cores, and distal occlusions, treatment decisions in incapacitated acute stroke patients must carefully balance trial evidence with individual premorbid function, personal values, and anticipated quality of life.

title: Mechanical Thrombectomy 24 to 72 Hours after Large-Vessel Ischemic Stroke

journal.name: The New England Journal of Medicine

abstract: Background: Endovascular thrombectomy is an established treatment for acute ischemic stroke. Whether the benefit extends to patients with salvageable brain tissue in the infarct who present more than 24 hours after symptom onset or the time when they were last known to be well is uncertain. Methods: We conducted an open-label, randomized trial with blinded outcome assessment at comprehensive stroke centers in China. Patients with acute ischemic stroke from large-vessel occlusion of the anterior circulation and imaging-identified salvageable brain tissue at 24 to 72 hours were assigned to receive endovascular therapy plus standard medical care (intervention group) or standard medical care alone (control group). The primary outcome was functional status, defined by the score on the modified Rankin scale (range, 0 to 6, with higher scores indicating greater disability and a score of 6 indicating death) at 90 days, with results assessed as the distribution of scores in each group. Secondary outcomes included disability, neurologic impairment, and safety. Results: A total of 336 patients were included in the intention-to-treat population, with 168 assigned to each group. The median time from symptom onset or from the point when the patient was last known to be well to randomization was 38.5 hours. Endovascular therapy resulted in a more favorable distribution of modified Rankin scale scores at 90 days than standard medical care alone (common odds ratio for a better functional outcome, 1.74; 95% confidence interval, 1.19 to 2.55). Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage occurred in 4.8% of the patients in the intervention group and in no patients in the control group, and the 90-day case fatality rate was 6.0% and 1.8%, respectively. Conclusions: Among patients who presented 24 to 72 hours after an acute ischemic stroke from large-vessel occlusion of the anterior circulation and had imaging-identified salvageable tissue, endovascular therapy resulted in better functional outcomes than standard care but led to a higher risk of intracranial hemorrhage and death. (Funded by the National Health Commission Capacity Building and Continuing Education Center and others; LATE-MT ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT05326932.)

ai_takeaways.conclusion_vi: In patients with anterior circulation large-vessel occlusion presenting 24 to 72 hours after symptom onset with salvageable tissue, mechanical thrombectomy improved 90-day functional outcomes (common OR, 1.74; 95% CI, 1.19 to 2.55) but increased the risk of symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage (4.8% vs. 0%) and 90-day mortality (6.0% vs. 1.8%).

title: Trial of Endovascular Therapy for Mild Stroke with Large-Vessel Occlusion

journal.name: The New England Journal of Medicine

abstract: Background: Although endovascular thrombectomy is the standard of care for acute ischemic stroke with moderate-to-severe symptoms caused by large-vessel occlusion, its efficacy and safety in patients presenting with mild stroke (National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale [NIHSS] score <6) remain uncertain. Methods: In this multicenter, prospective, randomized, open-label trial with blinded outcome assessment (MILD-MT), we randomly assigned patients presenting within 24 hours with acute mild ischemic stroke (NIHSS score <6) due to anterior-circulation large-vessel occlusion and salvageable tissue on perfusion imaging in a 1:1 ratio to receive endovascular therapy plus standard medical care or standard medical care alone. The primary outcome was the distribution of scores on the modified Rankin scale (range, 0 to 6, with lower scores indicating less disability) at 90 days, analyzed by ordinal logistic regression as a common odds ratio. Safety outcomes included symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage within 48 hours and 90-day mortality. Results: Endovascular therapy plus medical care resulted in a significantly more favorable distribution of modified Rankin scale scores at 90 days and a higher proportion of patients achieving functional independence (mRS 0–1) compared with standard medical care alone, preventing early neurological deterioration while maintaining an acceptable rate of symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage. Conclusions: Among patients with acute mild ischemic stroke (NIHSS <6) and anterior-circulation large-vessel occlusion, early endovascular thrombectomy plus medical management resulted in better 90-day functional outcomes than medical management alone.

ai_takeaways.conclusion_vi: In the randomized MILD-MT trial of patients with acute mild ischemic stroke (NIHSS <6) and anterior-circulation large-vessel occlusion, early endovascular thrombectomy plus medical care significantly improved 90-day functional outcomes (mRS distribution and mRS 0–1 rates) compared with medical management alone.

title: Association of Obesity With Intracranial Hemodynamic Alterations
abstract: BACKGROUND: Obesity increases the risk of stroke and cognitive decline, but its association with intracranial arterial hemodynamics remains unclear. We examined whether obesity score is associated with intracranial signal-intensity gradient, a time-of-flight magnetic resonance angiography–derived surrogate of arterial wall shear conditions, and whether this association differs by vascular territory. METHODS: This cross-sectional study included 5618 adults who underwent comprehensive health screening, including intracranial time-of-flight magnetic resonance angiography, in the Republic of Korea between 2012 and 2020. Body mass index was calculated from measured height and weight, and waist circumference was measured by health-screening staff on the same day as brain magnetic resonance angiography. An obesity score was calculated by assigning 1 point each for general and abdominal obesity, yielding scores of 0 (neither), 1 (either), or 2 (both). Arterial SIG and arterial radius were calculated using semiautomated 3-dimensional vessel segmentation. Lower SIG values were interpreted as reflecting reduced arterial wall shear conditions. Multivariable linear regression models assessed the association between obesity score and SIG across 11 intracranial arteries, adjusting for demographics, arterial radius, and cardiometabolic factors. RESULTS: Among 5618 participants (mean [SD] age, 55.9 [8.6] years; 45.2% women), higher obesity score was associated with lower SIG across all intracranial arteries ( P value for trend <0.001). In adjusted models, each 1-point increase in obesity score was associated with reduced SIG, including in the basilar artery (B=−0.26 [95% CI, −0.31 to −0.21]). The obesity-related reduction in SIG was greater in the posterior than anterior circulation and persisted after adjustment for arterial radius and cardiometabolic factors. CONCLUSIONS: A higher obesity score was associated with reduced intracranial arterial SIG, consistent with adverse time-of-flight magnetic resonance angiography–derived flow-related hemodynamic alterations. Greater reductions in the posterior circulation suggest territory-specific vulnerability, which may be associated with early cerebrovascular compromise in the context of obesity.

ai_takeaways.conclusion_vi: In this cross-sectional study of 5618 adults, higher obesity scores were independently associated with reduced intracranial signal-intensity gradients—surrogates for adverse arterial wall shear conditions—across all intracranial arteries (P<0.001), with greater reductions observed in the posterior circulation (e.g., basilar artery: B=-0.26 [95% CI, -0.31 to -0.21]).

title: Dual Versus Mono Antiplatelet Therapy in Mild Versus Moderate Ischemic Stroke: A Post Hoc Analysis of the ATAMIS Randomized Trial
abstract: BACKGROUND: This prespecified post hoc analysis of the ATAMIS trial (Antiplatelet Therapy in Acute Mild to Moderate Ischemic Stroke) aimed to investigate whether the benefit of dual antiplatelet therapy versus aspirin alone differs in patients with mild versus moderate stroke. METHODS: Using data from the modified intention‑to‑treat population of the ATAMIS trial, eligible patients were divided into mild (National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale [NIHSS] score 4–5) and moderate (NIHSS score 6–10) groups. The primary outcome was early neurological deterioration at 7 days, defined as an increase in the NIHSS score of ≥2 points from baseline. Safety outcomes included bleeding events and intracranial hemorrhage within 90 days. Binary logistic regression, Cox regression, and generalized linear models were used as appropriate. Adjusted models included age, sex, diabetes, hypertension, onset-to-treatment time, stroke cause, and other imbalanced baseline variables. Treatment-by-baseline stroke severity interaction was assessed. RESULTS: A total of 2915 patients were included, including 1992 (68.4%) with mild stroke and 923 (31.6%) with moderate stroke. Median age was 66 years (interquartile range, 59–73); 35.0% were women. Clopidogrel plus aspirin was associated with a significantly lower risk of early neurological deterioration compared with aspirin alone in the moderate stroke group (adjusted odds ratio, 0.31 [95% CI, 0.17–0.59]; P <0.001), whereas no significant difference was observed in the mild stroke group (adjusted odds ratio, 0.96 [95% CI, 0.66–1.41]; P =0.841). A significant interaction was identified between treatment effect and NIHSS score subgroup ( P interaction =0.003). The occurrence of bleeding events and intracranial hemorrhage was similar between treatment groups in both severity subgroups. CONCLUSIONS: In patients with acute mild-to-moderate ischemic stroke, the benefit of clopidogrel plus aspirin versus aspirin alone in preventing early neurological deterioration at 7 days may be greater among patients with moderate stroke (NIHSS score 6–10) than among those with mild stroke (NIHSS score 4–5), without an increased risk of bleeding. These findings suggest that baseline stroke severity may inform antiplatelet therapy selection, and warrant confirmation in future prospective studies. REGISTRATION: URL: https://www.clinicaltrials.gov ; Unique identifier: NCT02869009.

ai_takeaways.conclusion_vi: In acute ischemic stroke patients, dual antiplatelet therapy (clopidogrel plus aspirin) significantly reduced early neurological deterioration at 7 days compared to aspirin alone in moderate strokes (NIHSS 6–10: aOR 0.31, 95% CI 0.17–0.59, P<0.001; P-interaction=0.003), but not in mild strokes (NIHSS 4–5: aOR 0.96, 95% CI 0.66–1.41, P=0.841), without increasing bleeding risks.

title: Sleep-Disordered Breathing Is Associated With Adverse Short- and Long-Term Outcomes in Acute Ischemic Stroke and TIA: A Retrospective Cohort Study From the Bern Sleep-Stroke Registry
abstract: BACKGROUND: Sleep-disordered breathing (SDB) is common after ischemic stroke and has been associated with adverse outcomes, yet evidence from large stroke cohorts remains limited. We evaluated the association of SDB severity with all-cause mortality, major adverse cardio- and cerebrovascular events (MACCE), and 3-month functional outcome. METHODS: This retrospective cohort study included consecutive patients with ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack admitted to Inselspital Bern between 2017 and 2021 who underwent in-hospital respiratory polygraphy. SDB severity was classified according to the apnea-hypopnea index as mild (5–<15 events/h), moderate (15–<30 events/h), or severe (≥30 events/h). Outcomes included all-cause mortality, first postindex MACCE, and modified Rankin Scale scores at 3 months. Multivariable Cox and logistic regression models adjusted for age, sex, body mass index, vascular risk factors, admission National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale, intravenous thrombolysis, and mechanical thrombectomy. RESULTS: Among 1083 patients (mean age, 66.0±14.5 years; 62.6% male), SDB (apnea-hypopnea index ≥5 events/h) was present in 819 patients (75.6%), including mild (29.8%), moderate (22.9%), and severe (22.9%). Median follow-up was 51.1 months (interquartile range, 39.1–67.8) for mortality and 47.7 months (interquartile range, 36.9–65.5) for first postindex MACCE; 178 deaths and 153 of 880 patients experienced a first postindex MACCE. Severe SDB was independently associated with increased all-cause mortality (adjusted hazard ratio, 1.73 [95% CI, 1.04–2.89]). Mild, moderate, and severe SDB were associated with first postindex MACCE (adjusted hazard ratio, 1.78 [95% CI, 1.03–3.06]; 2.20 [95% CI, 1.26–3.84]; and 2.16 [95% CI, 1.23–3.78], respectively; P for trend=0.009). Moderate and severe SDB were associated with unfavorable 3-month functional outcome (adjusted odds ratio, 1.74 [95% CI, 1.01–3.04] and 2.48 [95% CI, 1.45–4.31], respectively; P for trend <0.001). CONCLUSIONS: Severe SDB was independently associated with all-cause mortality, whereas SDB severity was associated with first postindex MACCE and unfavorable 3-month functional outcome. Acute-phase SDB assessment may improve prognostic risk stratification.

ai_takeaways.conclusion_vi: In acute ischemic stroke and TIA, severe sleep-disordered breathing is independently associated with increased all-cause mortality (aHR, 1.73 [95% CI, 1.04–2.89]) and unfavorable 3-month functional outcomes (aOR, 2.48 [95% CI, 1.45–4.31]), while any SDB severity increases post-index MACCE risk, supporting acute-phase respiratory screening for prognostic stratification.

title: Associations of Alzheimer Disease and Related Dementia Neuropathologies With Timely Diagnosis of Dementia in Health Care Settings
abstract: Background and Objectives: Timely diagnosis of dementia is essential for clinical management and care planning, yet underdiagnosis remains widespread. We investigated whether specific underlying brain neuropathologies are associated with receiving a timely clinical diagnosis of dementia in routine health care settings. Methods: This retrospective cohort study linked data from 5 longitudinal clinical-pathologic cohorts at the Rush Alzheimer's Disease Center with Medicare claims data. Participants who developed incident dementia during annual evaluations, had Medicare fee-for-service coverage, and underwent brain autopsy were included. Postmortem neuropathologic evaluations assessed Alzheimer disease neuropathologic change (ADNC), limbic-predominant age-related TDP-43 encephalopathy neuropathologic change (LATE-NC), Lewy body (LB) pathology, and vascular brain pathologies. Timely diagnosis was defined as a Medicare claim for dementia within 3 years before to 1 year after cohort-diagnosed dementia onset. Multivariable logistic regression estimated associations adjusted for demographics and survival time. Results: Among 524 deceased participants with incident dementia (mean age at dementia onset 88.2 years; 73% female), only 54% received a timely clinical diagnosis in Medicare claims. In multivariable models, ADNC (OR 1.91, 95% CI 1.21–3.00) and moderate-to-severe LATE-NC (OR 1.83, 95% CI 1.25–2.68) were independently associated with higher odds of receiving a timely dementia diagnosis. In contrast, vascular brain pathologies (OR 0.94) and neocortical Lewy body pathology (OR 1.00) were not significantly associated with timely diagnosis. Conclusions: Nearly half of older adults with incident dementia do not receive a timely clinical diagnosis in routine health care settings. Patients with underlying Alzheimer disease or LATE-NC pathology are nearly twice as likely to be diagnosed timely compared with those driven by vascular or Lewy body pathologies.

ai_takeaways.conclusion_vi: Nearly half (46%) of older adults with incident dementia miss a timely diagnosis in routine care; underlying Alzheimer pathology (OR 1.91, 95% CI 1.21–3.00) and LATE-NC (OR 1.83, 95% CI 1.25–2.68) nearly double the odds of timely clinical recognition compared with vascular or Lewy body dementia.

title: Risk of Inflammatory Bowel Disease After Anti-CD20 Treatment in Multiple Sclerosis
abstract: Importance: Anti-CD20 biologics are widely used as disease-modifying therapy (DMT) for relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS), but recent reports have raised concerns about an increased risk of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) during treatment. This study aimed to assess treatment-associated IBD risk in individuals with RRMS. Objective: To compare the risk of new-onset IBD across different therapies for RRMS and relative to the general population. Design, Setting, and Participants: This was a population-based cohort study conducted in Sweden. Through the Swedish MS register, initiations of rituximab, natalizumab, dimethyl fumarate, and fingolimod were identified between January 1, 2011, and December 31, 2023, in individuals with RRMS aged 18 to 55 years with at least 10 years of lookback time (5 years for dispensed drugs) and no evidence of previous IBD. These initiations were matched with general population comparator episodes selected from the Swedish population. Exposures: Rituximab, comparator DMTs (natalizumab, dimethyl fumarate, fingolimod), or general population comparator. Main Outcomes and Measures: New-onset IBD, defined as 2 or more records on separate dates with the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems , Tenth Revision , codes K50 (Crohn disease), K51 (ulcerative colitis), and/or K52.3 (indeterminate colitis). Results: Among the 13 748 therapy episodes (6481 rituximab, 2976 natalizumab, 2767 dimethyl fumarate, 1524 fingolimod) in 9251 individuals (range in mean ages of the exposure groups, 35-38 years) and 61 065 matched general population episodes, 164 IBD events occurred during follow-up (40 with rituximab, 4 with comparator DMTs, and 120 in the general population). The crude incidence rate of IBD was 110 (95% CI, 76-147) per 100 000 person-years for rituximab, 13 (95% CI, 3-30) for the comparator DMTs, and 41 (95% CI, 34-48) for the general population. After adjustment for demographics and MS characteristics, the hazard ratio for the comparator DMTs vs rituximab was 0.10 (95% CI, 0.04-0.22). In the rituximab group, 62% of IBD events were classified as Crohn disease compared with 29% in the general population. The number needed to harm for rituximab vs the comparator DMTs was 131 (95% CI, 93-228) at 5 years, after full adjustment. Conclusions and Relevance: Results of this cohort study show that rituximab was associated with an increased risk of IBD compared with other modern MS therapies, after adjustment for differences in characteristics at therapy start. Clinicians and individuals with MS should consider IBD risk in treatment decisions and remain vigilant for gastrointestinal symptoms during anti-CD20 therapy.

ai_takeaways.conclusion_vi: Rituximab is associated with a significantly increased risk of new-onset inflammatory bowel disease compared with other modern multiple sclerosis therapies (adjusted HR vs. comparator DMTs, 0.10 [95% CI, 0.04-0.22]; number needed to harm at 5 years, 131 [95% CI, 93-228]). Neurologists should monitor patients on anti-CD20 therapy for gastrointestinal symptoms.
